topic.title: Fractional and negative indices (numbers)
topic.subject: maths
topic.examWeightHint: M8 Paper 1 (non-calculator), early to middle of the paper, almost every series. Two shapes recur: a three-part short-value question of 1 mark per part around Q8 (Summer 2025 Q8: a zero index, an index of minus one and an index of minus three) and a two-mark show-that index proof around Q11 (November 2025 Q11(b)). A single simplification carrying 3 marks also appears (Summer 2024 Q10). The calculator paper touches the same laws in one-mark items (Summer 2024 Paper 2 Q2), but the exact-value work belongs to Paper 1.
mustMemorise: a^(1/n) is the nth root of a, because n copies of it multiply to give a^1
a^(m/n) = (nth root of a)^m: the bottom number is the root, the top number is the power
Take the root first, then the power, so the arithmetic stays small enough for a non-calculator paper
a^(-n) = 1 over a^n, from a^n x a^(-n) = a^0 = 1; the answer is never negative when the base is positive
(a/b)^(-n) = (b/a)^n: a negative index turns a fraction upside down
notOnThisSpec: Logarithms, which appear in no CCEA GCSE Mathematics statement, so a^x = b is never solved that way
Fractional indices whose root is not exact: Paper 1 answers must be exact, so the bases chosen always have whole-number roots
Surd manipulation for its own sake, which belongs to M8-NA-01 and is a separate topic here

note.title: Fractional and negative indices

given: Nothing: the Higher formula sheet carries no index law, so every rule on this page has to be known
mustKnow: a^(1/n) = the nth root of a
a^(m/n) = (nth root of a)^m, bottom number the root and top number the power
a^0 = 1 for any non-zero a, and the zero index applies only to the symbol it sits on
The order that keeps the arithmetic small: sign, then root, then power

notOnThisSpec: Logarithms: they are in no CCEA GCSE statement
Fractional indices with inexact roots, because Paper 1 answers must be exact

mustBeAbleTo: Write down the value of a zero index, a negative integer index and a unit fractional index without working
Evaluate a^(m/n) by taking the nth root first and then the mth power, for bases whose root is exact
Evaluate a negative fractional index by writing the reciprocal line first, then the root, then the power
Apply a negative index to a fractional base by turning the fraction over and making the index positive
Give an exact answer as an integer or a fraction in its lowest terms, because Paper 1 allows no calculator
Reach a printed result in a show-that index question by a written chain of steps
Compare two index values without evaluating them as decimals, using the size of the denominators
Check a root forwards before using it, so a claimed fourth root is confirmed by raising it to the fourth power
sheet.howExamined: M8 Paper 1 only for the exact-value work (non-calculator, 1 hour 15 minutes, 50 marks; the formula sheet on page 2 carries no index law). Expect it early to middle: a three-part question worth 1 mark per part worded Write down the value of, and a two-mark Show that index proof. A single simplification for 3 marks also appears. Schemes award A1 per short value with no working demanded, and M1 A1 on the longer items, where the method mark is for the root or the reciprocal being seen and the accuracy mark for the exact value.
traps: Reading a negative index as a negative answer: minus eight for 2^(-3), minus one thousand for 10^(-3), Summer 2025 M8 Paper 1 Q8 and Summer 2025 M7 Paper 1 Q17
Multiplying the base by the index instead of powering it: minus thirty for 10^(-3), Summer 2025 M7 Paper 1 Q17
Losing the minus sign altogether between the question and the working, Summer 2025 M8 Paper 1 Q8
Swapping the two numbers of a fractional index, so the denominator becomes the power, November 2025 M8 Paper 1 Q11
Treating a fractional index as a multiplier, so 16^(3/4) becomes 16 times three quarters, November 2025 M8 Paper 1 Q11
Applying only the root or only the power and stopping, Summer 2024 M8 Paper 1 Q10
Applying a zero index to the whole term, so 5 times 12^0 is given as one, Summer 2025 M7 Paper 1 Q17
Squaring or cubing the base before taking the root, which makes the arithmetic impossible without a calculator

workedExamples.stem:
Work out the value of $27^{\frac{2}{3}}$.

You may not use a calculator.

steps.working: The index is $\frac{2}{3}$. The bottom number is $3$, the top number is $2$.
steps.decision: Before anything is worked out I read the two numbers separately. The denominator says which root; the numerator says which power. Splitting them is the whole method, and it is what the examiners say candidates who lose marks never do.

options: Because the denominator names the root and the numerator names the power
Because you always divide the base by the denominator
Because the two numbers must be added together first
whyMenu.explain: In $a^{\frac{m}{n}}$ the bottom $n$ is the root and the top $m$ is the power. Nothing is added and nothing is divided into the base.

steps.decision: Root first, because it makes the number smaller. Cubing $27$ first would give a five-figure number to take a cube root of afterwards, and this is the non-calculator paper.
Now the power. The answer is 9, a whole number, which is the usual sign that the root has been taken correctly.

workedExamples.stem:
Work out the value of $8^{-\frac{4}{3}}$.

Give your answer as a fraction in its lowest terms.

steps.decision: The minus sign is the first job and it is a separate one. A negative index means a reciprocal, never a negative answer, so I deal with it before I touch the fraction.

options: Because $a^{-n}$ means $\dfrac{1}{a^{n}}$, so the sign turns the power over
Because a minus index makes the answer negative
Because the base must be multiplied by the index
whyMenu.explain: From $a^{n} \times a^{-n} = a^{0} = 1$, the two must be reciprocals. That is where the rule comes from, and it is why the answer stays positive.

steps.decision: The bottom of the fraction index is $3$, so take the cube root of $8$. Root before power keeps the arithmetic small enough to do in your head.
The top of the fraction index is $4$, so raise 2 to the fourth power. That gives $8^{\frac{4}{3}} = 16$.
Put the 16 back under the $1$ from step 1. The answer is a positive fraction, which is what a negative index always gives when the base is positive.

twin.stem: Work out the value of $16^{-\frac{3}{4}}$, giving your answer as a fraction in its lowest terms.

workedExamples.stem:
Work out the value of $\left(\dfrac{25}{4}\right)^{-\frac{3}{2}}$.

Give your answer as a fraction in its lowest terms.

steps.decision: A negative index on a fraction turns the fraction upside down and makes the index positive. Doing that first removes the minus sign for good, so it cannot come back as a minus in the answer.
The bottom of the index is $2$, so take the square root. Root the top and the bottom separately: $\sqrt{4} = 2$ and $\sqrt{25} = 5$.
The top of the index is $3$, so cube what is left. Cube the numerator and the denominator separately.

twin.stem: Work out the value of $\left(\dfrac{49}{9}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}$, giving your answer as a fraction in its lowest terms.

steps.decision: A show-that question is marked on the chain, not on the last line, so every step has to be written. The minus sign goes first.
The denominator $5$ says fifth root. Checking rather than guessing: $3^{5} = 243$, so the fifth root is right.
The numerator $2$ squares it, and the reciprocal from step 1 puts it underneath. The last line matches the printed result, which is what the final mark is for.

twin.stem: Show that $1000^{-\frac{2}{3}} = \dfrac{1}{100}$. Then state the value of $1000^{\frac{2}{3}}$.

items.skill: Read a negative index as a reciprocal

options.feedback: Yes. $5^{-2} = \dfrac{1}{5^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{25}$. The minus sign turned the power over; it did not make anything negative.
The minus sign in an index does not make the answer negative. It means a reciprocal: $5^{-2} = \dfrac{1}{5^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{25}$. A positive base can never give a negative power.
Here the base and the index have been multiplied, giving $5 \times 2 = 10$ underneath. The index is a power, not a multiplier: square the $5$ first, then put it under $1$.
That is $5^{2}$, with the minus sign left behind. Write the reciprocal line $\dfrac{1}{5^{2}}$ before you work anything out and the sign cannot be lost.

items.skill: Read a unit fractional index as a root

options.feedback: Yes. $8^{\frac{1}{3}}$ is the cube root of $8$, because $2^{3} = 8$.
That is $8 \times \dfrac{1}{3}$. An index is never a multiplier. The $3$ underneath asks for the cube root, so the answer is 2.
The $3$ has been used as a power instead of a root. In $a^{\frac{m}{n}}$ the number underneath is always the root, so $8^{\frac{1}{3}} = \sqrt[3]{8} = 2$.

items.skill: Take the root, then the power, in a fractional index

options.feedback: The two numbers have swapped jobs: this is $64^{\frac{3}{2}}$, square root then cube. The bottom of the index is the root, so take the cube root of $64$ first.
Only the power has been used. $64^{2} = 4096$ is the halfway point of one wrong route; the cube root still has to be taken, and taking it first keeps the numbers small.
That is $64 \times \dfrac{2}{3}$. The index tells you what to do to $64$, not what to multiply it by: cube root, then square.

items.skill: Combine a negative sign with a fractional index

options.feedback: Yes. The minus turns it over and the $2$ underneath takes the square root: $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{16}} = \dfrac{1}{4}$.
The square root has been found correctly and then given a minus sign. A negative index makes a reciprocal, so the answer is 1/4, not a negative number.
That is $16^{\frac{1}{2}}$, with the minus left out. Writing $\dfrac{1}{16^{\frac{1}{2}}}$ as your first line protects that mark.
Here $16$ was multiplied by $\dfrac{1}{2}$ and then turned over. The $2$ underneath asks for a square root, which gives 4, so the answer is 1/4.

items.skill: Apply a negative index to a fraction

options.feedback: Yes. Turn the fraction over, then square: $\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{16}{9}$.
The fraction has been squared without being turned over first, so the minus sign has done nothing. Turn it over, then square.
The fraction has been turned over, which is the right first move, but the power of $2$ was never applied. Both jobs have to happen: turn over, then square.
A minus index does not put a minus sign on the answer. It flips the fraction, so the result is 16/9, which is bigger than $1$ because the base was less than $1$.
Yes. $10^{-3} = \dfrac{1}{10^{3}} = \dfrac{1}{1000}$, which is $0.001$ as a decimal.
This was the commonest wrong answer in the examiners' report for the Summer 2025 indices question. The minus sign turns the power over; it does not make it negative.
Here the base has been multiplied by the index, $10 \times 3$, and then made negative. An index counts how many tens are multiplied together, so $10^{3} = 1000$ and $10^{-3} = 1/1000$.
That is $10^{3}$. The minus sign has gone missing between the question and the working; writing the reciprocal line first stops that.

items.skill: Apply a zero index to the right part of a term

options.feedback: Yes. The zero index sits on the $12$ only, and $12^{0} = 1$, so the answer is $5 \times 1 = 5$.
The zero index has been applied to the whole term. It belongs to the $12$ alone, so the $5$ in front survives untouched.
Here $12^{0}$ has been read as $12$. Anything to the power zero is $1$, because $\dfrac{12^{n}}{12^{n}} = 12^{0}$ and a number divided by itself is $1$.
A power of zero does not make the term zero. $12^{0} = 1$, so $5 \times 12^{0} = 5$.

items.skill: All three jobs in one negative fractional index

options.feedback: Yes. Turn it over, cube root the $8$ to get 2, square that to get 4, so the answer is 1/4.
That is $8^{\frac{2}{3}}$: the root and the power are right, only the reciprocal is missing. One extra line, $\dfrac{1}{8^{\frac{2}{3}}}$, would have held that mark.
The root and the power are right. The minus sign means a reciprocal, so the $4$ goes underneath a $1$ rather than getting a minus sign.
The square has been used but the cube root has not: $8^{2} = 64$. Take the cube root first, then square, then turn it over.

hints: The $2$ underneath the index asks for a square root.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $9 \times \dfrac{1}{2}$. The index is an instruction, not a multiplier: the $2$ underneath means square root, so the value is 2.

hints: Which number cubed gives $64$?

commonErrors.feedback: The $3$ has been used as a power. In $a^{\frac{m}{n}}$ the number underneath is the root, so this is the cube root of $64$, which is 4.

parts.stem:
Write down the value of $3^{-2}$.

Give your answer as a fraction.
hints: A negative index means one over the positive power.

commonErrors.feedback: The minus sign belongs to the index, not to the answer. $3^{-2}$ means $\dfrac{1}{3^{2}}$, which is 1/9.

parts.stem:
Write down the value of $10^{-4}$.

Give your answer as a fraction.
hints: Count the zeros in $10^{4}$, then put the whole thing under $1$.

commonErrors.feedback: Here the base and the index were multiplied. $10^{4}$ counts four tens multiplied together, which is 10000, so $10^{-4} = 1/10000$.

hints: The bottom of the index is the root; the top is the power.
Square-root first: the numbers stay small.

commonErrors.feedback: The square root is right and it earns the method mark. The top of the index, $3$, still has to be used: cube the 5 to reach 125.

hints: A $4$ underneath means a fourth root.
$2^{4} = 16$, so the fourth root of $16$ is 2.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $16 \times \dfrac{3}{4}$. Take the fourth root of $16$ first, which is 2, then cube it.

parts.stem:
Work out the value of $8^{-\frac{2}{3}}$.

Give your answer as a fraction in its lowest terms.
hints: Sign first, then root, then power.
The cube root of $8$ is 2.

commonErrors.feedback: The root and the power are both right, so the method mark is safe. Only the reciprocal is missing: the answer is 1/4.

parts.stem:
Work out the value of $81^{-\frac{3}{4}}$.

Give your answer as a fraction in its lowest terms.
hints: A $4$ underneath means a fourth root; $3^{4} = 81$.
Cube the root, then put it under $1$.

commonErrors.feedback: The fourth root was taken correctly and then raised to the power $4$ instead of $3$. The top number is the power: cube the 3 to get 27.

hints: Square-root the top and the bottom separately.

parts.stem:
Work out the value of $\left(\dfrac{2}{5}\right)^{-3}$.

Give your answer as a fraction in its lowest terms.
hints: A negative index turns a fraction upside down.
Cube the top and the bottom separately.

commonErrors.feedback: The cube is right but the fraction was never turned over, so the minus sign did no work. Flip first: $\left(5/2\right)^{3} = 125/8$.

parts.stem:
Work out the value of $\left(\dfrac{16}{81}\right)^{-\frac{3}{4}}$.

Give your answer as a fraction in its lowest terms.
hints: Three jobs: turn over, fourth root, cube.
Root the top and the bottom of the fraction separately.
parts.workedSolution: Turning it over gives $\left(\dfrac{81}{16}\right)^{\frac{3}{4}}$. The fourth root is $\dfrac{3}{2}$, and cubing that gives $\dfrac{27}{8}$.

commonErrors.feedback: The fourth root and the cube are both right, so two marks stand. The fraction was not turned over, so the answer is the reciprocal of 27/8.

hints: Deal with the two powers separately before you divide.
Dividing by 1/16 is the same as multiplying by 16.
parts.workedSolution: $64^{\frac{2}{3}} = 16$ and $4^{-2} = \dfrac{1}{16}$. Dividing by \dfrac{1}{16} means multiplying by 16, so the value is $16 \times 16 = 256$.

commonErrors.feedback: The $64^{\frac{2}{3}}$ is right. The second power was treated as 16 rather than 1/16, so the division went the wrong way. A negative index makes a small number here, and dividing by it makes the answer larger.

context.setting: Three one-mark index values, as they open an M8 Paper 1 indices question

hints: Any number to the power zero has the same value.
parts.workedSolution: $7^{0} = 1$, because $\dfrac{7^{n}}{7^{n}} = 7^{0}$ and any number divided by itself is $1$.

commonErrors.feedback: A power of zero does not make the value zero. Subtracting equal indices gives $7^{0}$, and that must equal 1.

parts.stem:
Write down the value of $4^{-1}$.

Give your answer as a fraction.
hints: A power of $-1$ is the reciprocal.

commonErrors.feedback: The minus sign lives in the index. It asks for the reciprocal, so the value is 1/4.

parts.stem:
Write down the value of $2^{-5}$.

Give your answer as a fraction.
hints: Work out $2^{5}$ first, then put it under $1$.

commonErrors.feedback: Here the base and the index were multiplied. Five twos multiplied together give 32, so $2^{-5} = 1/32$. The examiners' report on the Summer 2025 paper named exactly this pattern as the difference between the middle and the top of the entry.

context.setting: A printed result to be reached, in the style of the short index proof on M8 Paper 1

scheme.for: $25$ reached and the reciprocal taken to give 1/25

hints: Start by writing the reciprocal, so the minus sign is dealt with and gone.
The cube root of $125$ is 5.
A show-that answer must reach the printed line by a chain, not start from it.

commonErrors.feedback: Squaring $125$ first gives a five-figure number, and the cube root of it still has to be taken. Both orders reach the same place, but on a non-calculator paper only root-first is workable. Take $\sqrt[3]{125} = 5$, then square.

emphasis: negative fractional index on a fraction

context.setting: Two index values, the second on a fractional base

hints: Square root first, because the bottom of the index is $2$.

commonErrors.feedback: The square root earns the method mark. The $3$ on top has still to be used: cube the 6 to reach 216.

parts.stem:
Work out the value of $\left(\dfrac{8}{27}\right)^{-\frac{2}{3}}$.

Give your answer as a fraction in its lowest terms.
hints: Turn the fraction over first and the minus sign is gone.
Cube-root the top and the bottom separately.
parts.workedSolution: Turning it over, $\left(\dfrac{8}{27}\right)^{-\frac{2}{3}} = \left(\dfrac{27}{8}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}$. The cube root is $\dfrac{3}{2}$, and squaring that gives $\dfrac{9}{4}$.

commonErrors.feedback: The cube root and the square are right, so two marks stand. The fraction was never turned over: the answer is the reciprocal, 9/4.

context.setting: Two labelled index expressions to be compared

parts.stem:
$A = 4^{-\frac{3}{2}}$ and $B = 27^{-\frac{2}{3}}$.

Work out which of $A$ and $B$ is the larger.

You must show your working.

accepted: A is larger: A = 1/8 = 0.125 and B = 1/9 = 0.111 to three decimal places
A is larger because A = 1/8 and B = 1/9, and 8 is less than 9

scheme.for: A identified as the larger, with a comparison seen
scheme.examinerNote: Both are fractions with numerator $1$, so the one with the smaller denominator is the larger: 8 is less than 9.

hints: Deal with each one on its own before comparing anything.
Root first, then power, then turn it over.
Two fractions with a numerator of $1$ compare by their denominators, the other way round.
parts.workedSolution:
$A = 4^{-\frac{3}{2}} = \dfrac{1}{4^{\frac{3}{2}}}$. Since $\sqrt{4} = 2$ and $2^{3} = 8$, $A = \dfrac{1}{8}$.

$B = 27^{-\frac{2}{3}} = \dfrac{1}{27^{\frac{2}{3}}}$. Since $\sqrt[3]{27} = 3$ and $3^{2} = 9$, $B = \dfrac{1}{9}$.

Both have numerator $1$, and 8 is less than 9, so $A$ is the larger.

commonErrors.feedback: If the minus signs are dropped, $A$ becomes 8 and $B$ becomes 9, and $B$ looks bigger. With the reciprocals in place the order turns round: the larger denominator gives the smaller value, so A is the larger.

findTheMistake.stem: Niamh was asked to work out the value of $16^{\frac{3}{4}}$ without a calculator. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: On line 2 the index has been treated as a multiplier: $16$ was multiplied by $\dfrac{3}{4}$. An index is an instruction about powers and roots, so the $4$ underneath asks for a fourth root and the $3$ on top asks for a cube.
findTheMistake.feedback: Nothing here is careless: the arithmetic is fine, and the same slip appears every series. What is missing is the meaning of the index. Read $a^{\frac{m}{n}}$ as two jobs before you write anything: root by the bottom number, power by the top. Then the fourth root of $16$ is 2, and cubing it gives 8. If you are unsure whether a root is right, check it forwards: $2^{4} = 16$.

findTheMistake.stem: Ruairí was asked to work out the value of $8^{-\frac{2}{3}}$, giving his answer as a fraction. His working:
studentWorking: the index is negative, so the answer is -4
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The root and the power on lines 1 and 2 are both correct and would earn the method mark. Line 3 reads the minus sign as a sign on the answer. A negative index means a reciprocal: $8^{-\frac{2}{3}} = \dfrac{1}{8^{\frac{2}{3}}}$.
findTheMistake.feedback: The method mark is safe, because the cube root and the square are exactly what the scheme wants to see. Only the last line costs you. The rule comes from $a^{n} \times a^{-n} = a^{0} = 1$: two numbers whose product is $1$ are reciprocals, so a negative index can never produce a negative answer from a positive base. Write the reciprocal line first, before any arithmetic, and the sign has nowhere to go wrong.

findTheMistake.stem: A candidate was asked to show that $81^{-\frac{3}{4}} = 1/27$. Their working:
studentWorking: 1/81 is not 1/27, so the statement is false
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Lines 1 and 2 are right. On line 3 the $4$ has been used twice: once as the root, which was correct, and again as the power. The top number, $3$, is the power, so it should be $3^{3}$.
findTheMistake.feedback: The reciprocal line and the fourth root are both worth having, and they carry the method mark. The habit that prevents the rest is to write the two numbers down separately before you use either of them: bottom is the root, top is the power. It also pays to distrust a show-that answer that comes out false. On this paper a printed result is almost always true, so a mismatch is a signal to re-read your own working rather than to write a conclusion.

prompts.answer: It is the $n$th root of $a$. Multiplying $n$ copies of $a^{\frac{1}{n}}$ adds the indices to give $a^{1} = a$, so $a^{\frac{1}{n}}$ must be the number whose $n$th power is $a$.

prompts.prompt: What does $a^{\frac{m}{n}}$ mean, and which of the two numbers do you use first?
prompts.answer: $a^{\frac{m}{n}} = \left(\sqrt[n]{a}\right)^{m}$: the bottom number is the root and the top number is the power. Take the root first, because it keeps the numbers small enough for a non-calculator paper.

prompts.prompt: What does a negative index mean, and why is the answer never negative?
prompts.answer: $a^{-n} = \dfrac{1}{a^{n}}$. It comes from $a^{n} \times a^{-n} = a^{0} = 1$, so the two are reciprocals. A positive base raised to any power stays positive, so the reciprocal is positive too.
Turn it over, cube-root the $8$ to get 2, raise to the fourth power to get 16: the answer is $\dfrac{1}{16}$.

prompts.prompt: A question gives you $a^{-\frac{m}{n}}$ where $a$ is a fraction. In what order do you do the three jobs?
prompts.answer: Turn the fraction over (the minus sign), then take the $n$th root of the top and the bottom, then raise both to the power $m$. Doing the sign first means it cannot reappear as a minus in the answer.

prompts.prompt: Why is $2^{-3}$ not $-8$, and not $-6$ either?
prompts.answer: $2^{-3} = \dfrac{1}{2^{3}} = \dfrac{1}{8}$. Writing $-8$ treats the index sign as the answer's sign; writing $-6$ multiplies the base by the index. The index counts how many twos are multiplied, and the minus turns that upside down.

prompts.prompt: What is the value of $9 \times 5^{0}$, and where does the zero index apply?
prompts.answer: $5^{0} = 1$, and the zero index sits on the $5$ only, so the value is 9. A number in front of the power is untouched unless it is inside a bracket.

prompts.prompt: On the M8 papers, which index facts are printed on the formula sheet?
prompts.answer: None of them. The Higher formula sheet gives the volume and area formulae, the quadratic formula and the three trigonometry rules. Every index law has to be known, so no mark here is ever for quoting a rule.

prompts.prompt: Without working out either value, which is larger: $5^{-2}$ or $2^{-5}$?
prompts.answer: $5^{-2} = \dfrac{1}{25}$ and $2^{-5} = \dfrac{1}{32}$. Both have numerator $1$, so the one with the smaller denominator is the larger: $5^{-2}$.

findings.asked: Three short index values in one question: a zero index, an index of minus one and an index of minus three.
findings.wentWrong: The report describes this question as differentiating by ability: most of the entry handled the zero index, many handled the index of minus one, and only the stronger candidates handled the index of minus three.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Wrote the reciprocal line first for each negative index, so the minus sign was dealt with before any arithmetic began.
findings.rule: A negative index means one over the positive power. Write that line down before you work anything out.

findings.asked: An index simplification and a short numerical index proof in the same question.
findings.wentWrong: On the proof, fewer than half the entry built an argument the examiners were willing to accept, and more than half showed no grasp of what the two numbers in the index were there to do.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Split the fractional index into its two jobs on the page: the number underneath as the root, the number on top as the power, each on its own line.
findings.rule: In a show-that question the marks are on the chain of steps, so write the root and the power as separate lines.

findings.asked: A single index simplification carrying three marks.
findings.wentWrong: Examiners called the response very mixed, and the slips were of many different kinds: roughly a quarter of the entry took every mark and roughly a quarter took none.
findings.rule: Do one index job per line. Mixed errors come from trying to do the root, the power and the sign in a single step.

findings.asked: Four short index values, including a zero index on a term with a number in front of it.
findings.wentWrong: The report lists the commonest wrong answers part by part, and they are all sign or meaning errors rather than arithmetic: a value of minus eight for one part, minus one thousand or minus thirty for another, and an answer that still contained the letter for the zero-index part.
findings.rule: A zero index applies only to the symbol it sits on, and a minus index turns a power over rather than making it negative.

insight.ruleToRemember: Read the index before you touch the base: the minus sign means turn it over, the bottom number is the root, the top number is the power. Three small jobs, in that order, each on its own line.
insight.aStarSignal: Handling a negative fractional index on a fractional base in one clean chain, and being able to compare two such values without evaluating them as decimals.
